passages.text: LIGHT, that principle by which objects are made perceptible to our sense of seeing; consisting, according to Sir Isaac Newton, of exceedingly small particles emitted from luminous bodies.
Others, after Huygens, suppose it to be the vibrations of a subtle elastic medium which fills all space; but the Newtonian opinion is now generally received.
Its motion is not instantaneous: from the eclipses of Jupiter's satellites, Roemer, and after him Dr Bradley, found that it comes from the sun to the earth in about eight minutes.
White light is not simple but compounded of rays of different colours, which are separated by the prism, as Newton demonstrated.
Light is reflected from the surfaces of bodies, and refracted, or bent, in passing out of one medium into another of different density.
Some chemists hold that light is a substance which combines with bodies, and is the cause of the green colour of plants.
Light is electromagnetic radiation that can be perceived by the human eye.

Light shows properties of both waves and particles. In the 19th century the wave theory of Huygens, supported by Young and Fresnel, replaced Newton's corpuscular theory; in the 20th century light was found to come in quanta called photons.

The speed of light in a vacuum is about 300,000 kilometres per second. Ole Romer first showed in 1676, from the timing of eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io, that light travels at a finite speed. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
Isaac Newton showed with prisms that white light is a mixture of colours, which a prism separates into a spectrum.
Light is reflected at surfaces and refracted, changing direction, when it passes from one medium into another.
The idea of a luminiferous aether filling space, in which light waves travel, was abandoned after the Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 and Einstein's theory of relativity.
Plants capture the energy of light in photosynthesis.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: Huygens, Newton, Jupiter's satellites, prism, refraction.
Speed of light scores well but covers one section of the entry, so it is a second candidate.

alignments.label: Particles

britannica.quote: exceedingly small particles emitted from luminous bodies

wikipedia.quote: light was found to come in quanta called photons

alignments.note: Newton's particles were set aside in the 19th century, then partly returned as photons.

alignments.label: Waves in a medium

britannica.quote: the vibrations of a subtle elastic medium which fills all space

wikipedia.quote: The idea of a luminiferous aether filling space

alignments.note: Huygens was right about waves, but the medium that filled space was abandoned.

alignments.label: Newton's view prevails

britannica.quote: the Newtonian opinion is now generally received

alignments.note: True in 1797, no longer: the wave theory won a few decades later.

alignments.label: Finite speed

wikipedia.quote: light travels at a finite speed

alignments.note: Same finding, from the same method: Jupiter's moons.

alignments.label: Eight minutes from the sun

britannica.quote: comes from the sun to the earth in about eight minutes

wikipedia.quote: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth

alignments.note: The 1797 figure is close to today's.

britannica.quote: compounded of rays of different colours, which are separated by the prism

wikipedia.quote: white light is a mixture of colours, which a prism separates

alignments.label: Reflection and refraction

britannica.quote: refracted, or bent, in passing out of one medium into another

wikipedia.quote: refracted, changing direction, when it passes from one medium into another

alignments.note: Same law in the same words.

alignments.label: Light and plants

britannica.quote: is the cause of the green colour of plants

wikipedia.quote: Plants capture the energy of light in photosynthesis

alignments.note: Light does matter to plants, but as a source of energy, not as a substance that colours them.

alignments.label: Electromagnetic
alignments.note: The link between light and electricity came in the 1860s.

suggestedQuestions: Who was right about light in 1797, Newton or Huygens?
How fast did people in 1797 think light travels?

Who was right about light in 1797, Newto.answer: Both, in part. In 1797 Newton's particle theory was generally received over Huygens's vibrations of a space-filling medium [B1] [B2]. Wikipedia says the wave theory replaced Newton's in the 19th century, and that in the 20th light was found to come in particles called photons [W2]. The medium Huygens assumed was abandoned [W6].

How fast did people in 1797 think light.answer: Fast but not instantly: from the eclipses of Jupiter's moons, light was found to come from the sun in about eight minutes [B3]. Wikipedia gives about 8 minutes 20 seconds, at about 300,000 kilometres per second [W3].
